correct.description: Option A is the equality operator and can be used on numeric primitives, boolean values, and object references. Options B and C are both arithmetic operators and cannot be applied to a boolean value. Option D is the logical complement operator and is used exclusively with boolean values. Option E is the modulus operator, which can only be used with numeric primitives. Finally, option F is a relational operator that compares the values of two numbers.

The value x + y is automatically promoted to int, so int and data types that can be promoted automatically from int will work. Options A, B, D are such data types. Option C will not work because boolean is not a numeric data type. Options E and F will not work without an explicit cast to a smaller data type.

In this example, the ternary operator has two expressions, one of them a String and the other a boolean value. The ternary operator is permitted to have expressions that don’t have matching types, but the key here is the assignment to the String reference. The compiler knows how to assign the first expression value as a String, but the second boolean expression cannot be set as a String; therefore, this line will not compile.

The code will not compile as is, so option A is not correct. The value 2 * x is automatically promoted to long and cannot be automatically stored in y, which is in an int value. Options B, C, and D solve this problem by reducing the long value to a smaller data type.

The code compiles and runs without issue. The post-increment operator (++) on line 4 returns the current value and then increments it, but the result is not assigned. On line 5, the pre-increment operator increments the value first and then returns it. The same logic applies to the decrement operators.

The expression in the if statement must be a boolean. In this case, it is an assignment (x = 5), which returns the value 5 (an int). This causes a compilation error because an int cannot be converted to a boolean.
The code uses the short-circuiting OR operator (||). Since the first expression (x > 2) is true, the second expression (y++ < 10) is never evaluated. Therefore, y remains 10.
A switch statement can accept primitive types like byte, short, char, and int, as well as their wrapper classes and Enums or Strings. It cannot accept long, float, double, or boolean.
The loop will run indefinitely because the termination condition (i < 10) is never met. The variable i is decremented in each iteration.
The break statement exits the loop, and the program continues with the next statement after the loop. The continue statement stops the current iteration and goes to the next one.
For a while loop, the condition is checked before the body is executed. For a do-while loop, the body is executed at least once before the condition is checked.
The nested loops iterate through the rows and columns. The if statement with the continue label affects the outer loop based on the values of row and col.
These are the correct results for the given bitwise operations. Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of the integer values.
The code uses a label with a break statement to exit multiple levels of nested loops at once. This is a valid Java construct.
The code fails to compile because the variable declared in the for-each loop is already declared in the same scope.
The cast (byte) is required because adding two bytes results in an int. Without the cast, the code will not compile.
The logical XOR operator (^) returns true only if exactly one of the operands is true. If both are true or both are false, it returns false.

On the third iteration, row = 2 and col = 2, so the expression on line 6 is true and the continue ends the outer loop with count still at 1. On the fourth iteration, row = 3 and col = 1, so the expression on line 6 is false, the continue is skipped, and count is incremented to 2. Finally, on the fifth and final iteration, row = 3 and col = 2, so the expression on line 6 is true and the continue ends the outer loop with count still at 2. The result of 2 is displayed, so the answer is option B.

Prior to the first iteration, m = 9, n = 1, and x = 0. After the iteration of the first loop, m is updated to 8, n to 3, and x to the sum of the new values for m + n, 0 + 11 = 11. After the iteration of the second loop, m is updated to 7, n to 5, and x to the sum of the new values for m + n, 11 + 12 = 23. After the iteration of the third loop, m is updated to 6, n to 7, and x to the sum of the new values for m + n, 23 + 13 = 36. On the fourth iteration of the loop, m > n evaluates to false, as 6 < 7 is not true. The loop ends and the most recent value of x, 36, is output, so the correct answer is option D.
